## B-111 — BUILT 2026-10-22, seen on the iPad 2026-10-22. A letter he had read could not be opened again with no connection, and each opening fetched it again; Mail keeps the letters it has downloaded

Built in the `feat-kept` worktree, off `featAB-int` (master at 88ef40d
with B-100 to B-105). D-016's phase 2. The owner, 2026-10-22: "No, no,
no, we should have print on there. All three are still wanted." (Print,
his photos in the body, and this.)

**What Mail does.** Apple: "When you make an iOS or iPadOS backup in
iCloud or iTunes, it backs up your mail settings, but not your email",
and "If you delete or change your email account settings, previously
downloaded email might be removed from your device"
(support.apple.com/en-us/102556). So Mail keeps the mail it has
downloaded on the device, out of the backup, and may lose it when the
account changes. Apple does not say more; its forums and a vendor's
pages say Mail reads offline the letters it has downloaded, keeps a file
once it has been opened, has no setting to download everything, and
opens a letter it has at once from its own copy
(discussions.apple.com/thread/7156936,
cleanor.app/reference/mail-storage-ios). A letter written offline waits
in the Outbox and goes when the connection is back, as the app's Outbox
already does (B-072). How many letters Mail keeps, and for how long, is
not known; the 300 and the 64 MB are D-016's. No source says Mail marks
a letter read from its own copy, and none is marked here.

**What it was.** D-016's phase 1 kept the folders and the first pages.
A letter's body was fetched every time it was opened, `BODY.PEEK[]` in
one FETCH, and with no connection a letter he had read a minute before
said "This message could not be downloaded." and "Can't connect to mail
server.". Only the last letter fetched was in memory (`lastBody`), for
its pictures and a forward's files.

**Changed.**

- *The store.* `KeptLetters` (Mail/KeptLetters.swift), made by the shelf
  over its own directory as `MailShelf.letters`, touching nothing on disk
  until its first use, at a letter opened, kept or gone, never before a
  launch's first frame. One file a letter in
  `Kept/<account>/letters/`, the bytes of `BODY.PEEK[]` exactly as the
  FETCH returned them, named `<hash of the folder>-<validity>-<uid>-
  <message>.eml`, and an index, `Kept/<account>/letters.json`: format 1
  of its own, `next`, and a record a letter, its folder, UIDVALIDITY, UID,
  Gmail id, bytes, CRC-32, its opening's number and its file. Read whole
  and written whole, atomically. An index of another format, or one that
  cannot be read, is nothing kept, and goes with every letter. At the
  first use, a file no record names goes (a crash between a letter's file
  and its record, an atomic write's leftover, an eviction cut short), a
  record whose file is missing is dropped, and a record naming a file not
  its own, one for a letter twice, or more than the bounds hold, is read
  within the rules. Every write, read and removal goes on the shelf's disk
  queue (`MailShelf.disk`, now the letters' too), in order with the wipe
  and the discard. The shelf's life reaches it through a test of the
  shelf's root and generation alone, so a shelf retired at a password
  save is freed with its letters. Every directory it makes, `Kept/`, the
  account's and `letters/`, is marked out of backup as it is made, by the
  helper the shelf's own writes use (`MailShelf.excludeFromBackup`), so
  `letters.json` is never in a backup whichever store wrote first.
- *The bounds.* 300 letters and 64 MB, the least recently opened going
  first, by a counter each keep and each showing bumps, never the clock;
  no letter over 5 MB, `IMAPMailRepository.largeLetterBytes`, the size
  above which a letter is opened in parts (B-054); keeps waiting for the
  disk at most 16 MB, one past it dropped; and a floor of 512 MB free on
  the volume (iOS's `volumeAvailableCapacityForOpportunisticUsage`, read
  through URLs made afresh at each reading, since a URL held from one
  reading to the next can keep what it read the first time; nil off iOS
  or where it cannot be read, which keeps): a letter that would
  leave less is not kept, every kept letter goes, said once, and nothing
  more is kept in that launch.
- *The check.* Every read looks up the four keys and reads the file in
  one block on the disk queue, and checks its size and CRC-32 against the
  record. Anything else drops the letter, record and file, and the
  opening goes to the server, where the letter is kept again.
- *A keep.* Its file is written, then the index with it and the letters
  it evicts, each atomically; only then, the shelf still alive and no
  discard come meanwhile (an epoch looked at again), does memory take the
  index, and only then do the evicted files go. An index that cannot be
  written takes the new file back; a file that cannot be written keeps
  nothing; either way the index on disk names only files written whole.
- *Keeping.* `MailRepository.openLetter(_:)`, a requirement of the
  protocol with a default that calls `loadMessage`, is what the reading
  pane calls in its three places: the letter tapped (`show(summary:)`), a
  conversation's newest (`show(thread:)`), and a letter of it opened, the
  unread ones with the newest and arrivals among them (`loadBody`). In
  `IMAPMailRepository` it fetches as `loadMessage` does, byte for byte on
  the wire, and keeps the letter after the whole FETCH has come and the
  letter is made, when the opening has not been called off, the server
  has named the letter under this UID in this launch and it is the row's,
  it is not empty and not over 5 MB, and the Drafts folder's name is known
  and the row is neither in it nor counted there. Otherwise one note says
  why: `KEPT-LETTER not-kept reason=size|unnamed|draft|cancelled`. A
  letter opened in parts is never kept. `loadMessage` and `loadDraft`
  keep nothing.
- *Kept first.* `openLetter` looks in the copy first, with no connection
  made and nothing sent, as Mail shows a letter it has: the row's Gmail
  id, its folder's name found without the wire (from LIST's roles once
  LIST has been had, otherwise the kept folder list), not a draft, and
  `seen` naming neither another UIDVALIDITY for the folder nor another
  letter under the UID. The letter is made by the very code a fetched one
  is (`Self.letter`), and is not the server's word: `lastBody` is not set,
  and neither `seen` nor the shelf's vouching is told, so a read mark,
  flag, move or delete on it is asked about first, as on any row this
  launch has not had. Where `seen` names another letter the opening goes
  on to the server's path, which refuses it with nothing sent, as before,
  and the refusal takes the kept letter (`MailShelf.refuse`).
- *Pictures and files.* The public `fetchAttachmentData` serves a part of
  a letter shown from the copy from it, matched by folder and id: from
  the letter last shown so, held in memory beside `lastBody`, or from the
  file of one of the 64 shown before it in the launch, read again and
  checked. Before `lastBody`, which is matched by the id alone, and which
  a letter shown from the copy never becomes, so the letter fetched last,
  another folder's under the same "<uidvalidity>/<uid>", would have
  answered for it. A letter fetched from the server under the same folder
  and id takes its place, so after a first page that disowns the copy the
  server's letter under that id shows its own pictures. A move or a
  delete forgets it, as a move forgets `lastBody`.
- *What goes, and when.* The least recently opened past the bounds; a
  letter the server has taken out of a folder, by `MailShelf.gone`
  (a delete, a move, a letter binned or marked as spam out of every folder
  but that one, an EXPUNGE from the Trash, a draft removed), whether or
  not a page holds its row; a move out of All Mail to a label takes
  nothing; a letter the server says is another (`refuse`); one whose
  check fails; and all of them with the copy, at a discard (the shelf
  calls `letters.forget()` before it removes the directory), a password
  saved or the account taken out and a safe start (the wipe of `Kept/`),
  another account's directory at launch, an index of another format, and
  the floor. Never at a relaunch, going offline or a Refresh.
- *Nothing sent.* The copy is read in two places, `keptLetter` and
  `keptPart`. A Forward's files and pictures, a draft's APPEND and every
  part a letter being built carries come from the server by folder, UID
  and X-GM-MSGID through `fetchCarried`, whose branch for a part naming no
  letter now calls `fetchAttachmentDataNotKept`, never the public function.
  `partOnScreen` reads `lastBody` alone. Offline such a letter waits in the
  Outbox (`cannotConnect`). A Reply or Forward quotes the words on screen,
  which are the server's own letter, checked, as from a letter fetched in
  the same launch; built so, the owner's question's default.
- *The log.* `KEPT-LETTER shown bytes=<n> ms=<n>`, `kept bytes=<n>
  ms=<n> free-ms=<n>` (the free-space reading's own part of the keep's
  time), `not-kept reason=…`, `dropped reason=check`, `cleared
  reason=space`: numbers and a word, never a folder, a UID, a Message-ID, a subject or a name. A
  showing sends nothing, so nothing of it reaches the wire log.

**Not changed.** `loadMessage`, its signature and its wire, and what calls
it: his letters from Sent Mail in a conversation's stack (B-104), which
are never kept. A letter over 5 MB, opened in parts, and B-097, its file
fetched again each time. Drafts. No queue of offline changes: a read mark
made offline puts the dot back, as before. The pages kept by phase 1 and
`Local Drafts/`, which nothing here touches.

**What he sees.** A letter he has opened before opens at once, with or
without a connection, its pictures that came in the letter and its files
with it. Pictures the letter loads from the web do not show offline, as
in Mail. A letter he never opened, and one over 5 MB, say what they say
today. No new words.

**Tests.** `KeptLettersTests`, 26, the store through the shelf that
makes it: a letter read back only under its four keys; the bounds, D-016's;
the 301st taking the least recently opened, a showing making a letter the
newest, a second keep only touching; the bytes bounded, and a letter over
5 MB not kept and taking nothing; a file changed by a byte, cut short,
grown or missing nothing and gone, and a byte changed found by the CRC-32
alone; an index of another format, cut short or not JSON nothing kept, its
files gone, a keep after working; an index outside the rules read within
them; the sweep at the first use, and nothing touched as the shelf is made;
a relaunch in the order opened, the counter going on; the wipe and the
discard, each with a keep on its way (a queue held), and a discard between
a keep's files and its memory (the keep held between the two); another
account's letters; the floor, said once, nothing more kept in the launch,
and nil free space keeping; a file where `letters/` goes, and an index that
cannot be written taking the new file back; keeps past 16 MB waiting
dropped; gone by UID and a letter binned from every folder but the bin;
refused; the flush; a shelf freed with its letters; the directories made
and marked out of backup by the shelf's helper, read from the source;
nothing of a letter in the log; the kept note timing the free-space
reading on its own beside the whole keep, and the app's reading making its
URLs afresh each time, read from the source; and a 5 MB letter kept in
58 ms and read back checked in a median 46 ms, in the debug build, printed.
`KeptLetterOpeningTests`, 23, over the shipping repository: opened online,
the FETCH `loadMessage`'s byte for byte, and again with nothing sent;
opened on a socket that died while the iPad slept, the FETCH lost in it
and sent again once on the new connection, as `loadMessage`'s is, and the
letter kept; the
next launch from the kept rows, online and offline, through the protocol
as the pane calls it, with no command at all, not even the LOGIN, each
showing the newest after; a letter never
opened failing offline as today; the letter from the copy the fetched one
field by field, and the pane's page and the stack's body the same, for
plain, HTML, both, related with a `cid:` picture, a picture and a file,
ISO-8859-1, encoded words and no Date; not shown where the server has
named another letter under the UID, refused with nothing sent and the
kept letter taken, nor where it has given the folder another UIDVALIDITY,
nor for another Gmail id or none; none shown after a first page that says
the copy was another mailbox's; a read mark, flag, move and delete on a
letter shown from the copy each asked about first; never kept: in parts,
a draft, a row counted in Drafts, a row with no Gmail id, another letter,
an opening called off, the letter in parts opened with the commands
`loadMessage` sends for it, its structure first and never the whole
letter; `loadMessage` and `loadDraft` keeping nothing,
`loadMessage`'s wire unchanged with a copy present; a Forward of a letter
shown from a kept file altered with its CRC made to match carrying the
server's bytes, named by X-GM-MSGID and, a part naming no letter, by folder
and UID, the same for its draft in Drafts, and waiting offline; its
pictures and files from the copy with nothing sent, offline, and not under
the same id in another folder; a picture of a letter shown from the copy
its own, never that of another folder's letter under the same
"<uidvalidity>/<uid>" fetched last (`lastBody`); a letter fetched under
the id of one shown from the copy serving its own picture; Delete, Trash,
Spam and EXPUNGE taking it and All Mail to a label not; a letter shown
from the copy and then moved to Spam, and another erased from the Trash,
giving no file from memory under the folder and id each had; a password
saved, the old
repository's keep landing nowhere; nothing of it in the log; and, read
from the source, the pane's three calls and his Sent Mail by `loadMessage`,
the requirement in the protocol itself, the copy reached in three places
alone, `keptLetter` setting no `lastBody` and telling no `seen` or vouching,
`fetchCarried` never through the public function, `partOnScreen` reading
`lastBody` alone, and nothing named in the screens, Local Drafts, the
Outbox, SMTP or the share extension.

Each rule undone in the worktree, one at a time, and the two classes run,
45 tests. Shown without the Gmail id compared: 6 failures in 3 tests.
Shown over `seen`: 7 in 2. No CRC: 7 in 2. `lastBody` set by a showing: 13
in 3. `saw` called by a showing: 2 in 2. A keep in `loadMessage`: 4 in 2.
A cancelled open kept: 2 in 1. Eviction by count alone: 3 in 1. `gone` not
reaching the letters: 11 in 2. The floor ignored: 6 in 1. No sweep of the
files no record names: 2 in 2. `fetchCarried` through the public
function: 4 in 2. `keptPart` matched by id alone: 5 in 2. The epoch not
looked at again before memory takes a keep: 1 in 1. A letter fetched under
the id of one shown from the copy not taking its place: 1 in 1. No cap on
the keeps waiting: 3 in 1. A failed index write leaving the new file: 1 in
1. A discard not forgetting the letters: 7 in 3. Drafts kept: 3 in 1. A
refusal not reaching the letters: 3 in 2. A showing not counted as an
opening: 2 in 2. The directories not marked out of backup: 1 in 1. The
pane's conversation opening by `loadMessage`: 3 in 1. `openLetter` only in
the protocol's extension: 6 in 2. A row whose Gmail id is not the one the
server named kept: 2 in 1.

Four tests more since, the in-parts case of the never-kept test made to
compare the wire with `loadMessage`'s, and each rule they hold undone the
same way, the two classes at 49 tests. `openLetter` fetching whole
whatever the size, which would bring back B-054's hang above 5 MB: 3
failures in 1 test. `openLetter` without the read retry, so the first

`lastBody` asked before the copy, as the spec had it: 2 in 1. A move not
forgetting the letter shown from the copy: 2 in 1. An EXPUNGE not

2 in 1. The reading not timed on its own: 2 in 1.

The full suite, serially: 2,029 tests, 5 skipped, none failing. The
release build for the iPad links.

**Not covered.**

- The iPad's free-space reading, and a disk really full: the host has
  neither, so the floor and a failed write are tried through what the
  store is handed.
- Years of churn beyond the bounds tests: the eviction, the orphan sweep
  and the format check are tried on hundreds of letters, not hundreds of
  thousands.
- How many letters Mail itself keeps, and for how long.
- Pictures the letter loads from the web, offline.
- The same letter opened from two folders, the Inbox and a search of All
  Mail, is kept twice, under each folder's keys, and counts twice against
  the bounds.
- A Forward of a kept letter whose original has gone from the server and
  from All Mail meanwhile fails with its parts missing, kept in the Outbox
  saying so, where a letter fetched in the same launch would have carried
  them from `lastBody` (PERFORMANCE.md). *Since B-107, one whose original
  he deleted is found in the Trash.*
- The hitch: a page read from the main thread can wait on the shared disk
  queue behind a letter's write of up to 5 MB and a free-space reading.
  Timed on the iPad by the kept note's ms, and the reading's own part by
  its `free-ms`, step 8 of the check: 44 to 58 ms of each keep was the
  reading, 70 to 90% of it (below). If that is slow, it can be read once a
  launch or every few minutes instead.
- The move's and the erasing's forgetting of the letters shown before the
  last (the 64 of this launch, read again from their files): no test can
  tell it, since the letter's record goes with it (`gone`) and its file
  is then read as nothing, except after a move out of All Mail to a
  label, where the letter is still under that UID and the copy still its
  own. The letter last shown, held in memory, is tested.
- A letter deleted in another client stays until it is evicted, reachable
  only from a kept row: the server's last word.
- The check on the simulator. On the iPad, below.

**Seen on the test iPad, 2026-10-22**, a build of int11 (e739d2c), iPadOS
16.5.1, three panes, the test account; P, H, F, L, N and two 3 MB letters
made on the host and put in its Inbox, and T a conversation of his letter

## B-112 — FIXED 2026-10-22, found on the iPad and seen there fixed but for the flag. A mark set on another device, told inside a Refresh's listing, made the letter's row "(unknown sender)", "(no subject)", 31/12/69, and split its conversation

**What he saw.** Seen on the test iPad on 2026-10-22, in B-102's check,
and made again three times in three the same morning. Organize by Thread
on, a conversation of two letters in the Inbox, the second a reply to the
first, on one row. From another IMAP connection on the test account,
`UID STORE +FLAGS (\Answered)` on the newer letter, then Refresh: the
conversation was two rows. The top one read "(unknown sender)", "(no
subject)" and 31/12/69, with the newer letter's words and the reply
arrow, and the older letter sat on its own under it. The next Refresh put
it right. It came once in four Refreshes after a mark set from the host,
and then every time: with the mark set, with it taken off, and with
Refresh tapped 2 s after the mark. On his iPad it would come whenever he
reads or answers a letter on another device and refreshes within a few
seconds.

Not by design. A row is its letter's sender, subject and date, in its
conversation, whatever else the server says.

**What it was.** Gmail's news, and the client's reading of it. RFC 3501
§7.4.2 lets a server send a FETCH at any time, and Gmail tells a connection
of a mark set elsewhere with one, `* 68 FETCH (UID 422 FLAGS (\Seen))`.
In three Refreshes of the first check's four it came on the NOOP a
Refresh sends before its SEARCH (B-045), and nothing went wrong. In the
fourth, and in all three tries made again that morning, it came inside
the listing's own `UID FETCH` answer, after the letter's whole line, once
some 5 s after the mark:

```
→ a048 UID FETCH 103,110,…,421:422 (UID FLAGS INTERNALDATE RFC822.SIZE ENVELOPE BODYSTRUCTURE X-GM-LABELS X-GM-THRID X-GM-MSGID)
← * 67 FETCH (X-GM-THRID … UID 421 … FLAGS (\Seen) ENVELOPE (…) …)
← * 68 FETCH (X-GM-THRID … UID 422 … FLAGS (\Answered \Seen) ENVELOPE (…) …)
← * 68 FETCH (UID 422 FLAGS (\Seen))
· SESSION-IDENT folder=INBOX uidv=1 exists=68 uids=68 first-row=1/422 msgid=-
```

That was `-FLAGS (\Answered)`: the whole line still carried the old
flags, and the news after it the new.

`IMAPParser.parseFetch` made each line a result of its own, so the news
was a result with a UID and flags and nothing else. `IMAPClient.ordered`,
which puts a listing's summaries in order, kept one per UID, the last: the
news. `IMAPMailRepository.rows(from:)` filled in what it lacked: "(unknown
sender)"; an empty subject, which the list shows as "(no subject)"; the
date 1970-01-01, which is 31/12/69 in the iPad's time zone; no Gmail
thread id, so the letter left its conversation; and no Gmail id,
`msgid=-`. The page kept on the iPad (D-016) was replaced with that row in
it. It was so from the first commit, older than B-102, whose marks set
elsewhere are exactly this news.

Every FETCH of one letter read the answer the same way and took the first
result under the UID, which with the news ahead of the letter's own line
is the news. Then the FETCH that vouches for a kept row (D-016) found no
Gmail id, so the write was not sent and the row came off the kept page as
another letter's; a kept row's letter opened was refused the same way; a
draft reopened by the id its upload gave it came with no bytes; a letter
too large to fetch whole had no structure, or was refused as another
letter; a file was refused the same way, or not found in the letter; and
the FETCH of a letter's labels after a hollow MOVE (B-092) found none,
so the MOVE was sent again. Not seen on the iPad, where the news came
after the letter's line. The previews and a letter's plain FETCH already
passed over a result with no bytes.

**Changed.**

- `IMAPParser.parseFetch` gives one result per UID. A later line for a UID
  already read is laid over it (`IMAPFetchResult.laying`): each item the
  later line carried in place of the earlier one's, the rest kept. So a
  news line changes the flags and nothing else, and the letter's sender,
  subject, date, Gmail ids, labels, structure, size and bytes stay. The
  later line has the say, the news after the letter's line or the letter's
  line after the news, as Gmail sends them in the order things happened. A
  line with no UID is left as it was.
- FLAGS and X-GM-LABELS go by whether the line carried them (`flagsSent`,
  `labelsSent`). `FLAGS ()`, every mark taken off, takes them off, where an
  empty list would have read as no FLAGS at all; a news line, which carries
  no X-GM-LABELS, leaves the labels, so the letter is still counted in
  Starred and in its labels' folders.
- `IMAPClient.ordered` merges again across the answers it is given, so
  news riding on one FETCH about a letter in another is laid over that
  letter too. A FETCH whose UIDs run past 7,000 characters goes in several;
  no list of the app's is that long today, but the rule holds there too.
- A summary with no ENVELOPE once merged is never made a row. It is news of
  a letter whose own line never came, its FETCH refused or the letter gone,
  or a line that came without the ENVELOPE asked for, and it is left out as
  a letter the FETCH did not answer for is:
  `FETCH-NO-ENVELOPE uid=422 left-out` in the connection log. So no row
  with no sender, subject or date reaches the list or the kept page. A
  page below the top fills itself from the UIDs after it, as for a letter
  gone; the page from the top comes back one short.
- Every place results are gathered by UID goes through it: the listing
  from the top and a date jump (`page`), the pages below and the watch's
  new letters (`fetchSummaries`), an All Mailboxes search's binned hits
  (`search(_:across:)`), the previews, a letter's whole bytes, plain,
  named and asked, the FETCH vouching for a kept row, a letter in parts,
  a file, and the labels after a hollow MOVE.

**Not changed.**

- What is sent: the same commands, no NOOP more, nothing asked again.
- News of a letter the FETCH did not ask for, one below the page, is not
  put on a row already on screen; the next listing that has the letter
  shows its marks, as before. News on a NOOP, a STORE or a MOVE is not read,
  as before.
- No new words.

**What he sees.** A letter read, flagged or answered on another device,
and Refresh at once: its row is the letter's, its sender, subject and
date, in its conversation, with the new mark if Gmail told of it inside
the listing, and with the mark it had until the next Refresh if Gmail held
the news back longer. The connection log's SESSION-IDENT names the
letter's Gmail id.

**Tests.** `FetchNewsTests`, seventeen, over the shipping repository and
client, the kept copy and the scripted server, whose `storeElsewhere` is a
STORE from another device and whose `flagNews` says where a connection
with the letter's mailbox open is told of it: on the next NOOP, as Gmail
did most times; ahead of the next UID FETCH's own lines; straight after
the letter's own line, which carries its old flags, as on the iPad, or
after the answer's first line for a letter the FETCH did not ask for; or
at the end of the answer, before its OK; and whose `envelopeless` leaves
the ENVELOPE out of a letter's line. All but the two over more than one
FETCH, and the one with no ENVELOPE, read off the connection log the app
keeps that the news came where they say, so none of them passes with no
news on the wire; the one with no ENVELOPE reads off it that the letter's
line came without one. And one in `IMAPParserTests` on the iPad's lines,
the names and ids made up, the letter's whole line with a structure and
bytes as well: with the news after it and with the news ahead of it, each
of its items is checked, the flags, labels, arrival, size, envelope,
structure, bytes and both Gmail ids.

- *Inside*, the iPad's: a conversation of two, the newer with a file in
  it, marked read elsewhere, then Refresh: NOOP, SEARCH, FETCH, the news
  straight after the letter's line, which carried no flags; the row whole,
  read, with its file and the paperclip and when it came, and in its
  conversation, the older as it was, SESSION-IDENT naming the letter's
  Gmail id, and the kept page the same, in memory and on disk.
- *Ahead:* the news first and the letter's line with the new flags: the
  row the letter's, when it came among it.
- *A launch's first listing:* the letter with a file marked read between
  the listing's SEARCH and its FETCH, the news ahead of its line, and
  again straight after it, where a Refresh would still have from the
  listing before what the line says: the row whole and read, the letter
  kept with it as large, in memory and on disk, and opened in parts, its
  file left on the server; the preview its text's.
- *At the end:* a letter in the middle of the page flagged elsewhere, the
  news after the fifty lines: the row whole and flagged, no other changed.
- *Marks taken off:* a letter with only `\Seen` marked unread elsewhere,
  its news `FLAGS ()`, and a flagged letter in Starred marked unread: both
  unread, the second still flagged and still counted in Starred.
- *Not asked for:* a letter below the page flagged elsewhere, told after
  the answer's first line, the page's oldest letter's: no row changed or
  added, and the page below has it flagged.
- *The watch:* a letter come, and marked read between the check's SEARCH
  and its FETCH: on the list whole and read.
- *A search:* a letter in the Trash flagged between the Trash's SEARCH and
  the FETCH of its hits: the binned hit whole and flagged.
- *Kept rows:* a read mark on a kept row with the news ahead of the
  vouching FETCH: the mark goes and the row stays kept. A kept row's
  letter opened with the news ahead: the letter.
- *One letter:* the news ahead of each FETCH the client makes of one
  letter, and again straight after the letter's line in each, both
  FETCHes of the letter in parts and of a file told so: its Gmail id, its
  bytes named, asked and plain, the letter in parts, its structure,
  header and text, a file, a preview and its summary, with its size, when
  it came, its file and its preview's part, each the letter's.
- *Labels:* a hollow MOVE from All Mail into the Inbox, the news ahead of
  the FETCH of its labels: labelled, one MOVE.
- *Two FETCHes:* an Inbox of 1,500, every summary asked for, two FETCHes.
  A letter of the first flagged once it is answered, the news inside the
  second: its summary whole and flagged. A letter of the second flagged,
  the news inside the first, and the second refused: no summary for it,
  every other whole, and the log line.
- *No ENVELOPE:* a letter of the first page and one of the page below
  whose lines come without it: neither a row. The first page one short,
  the kept page the same, in memory and on disk, and the log line; the
  page below fifty, filled from the letter after it, and its log line.

Each part undone in the worktree, one at a time, and the eighteen run,
counted as failures in tests. The code as it was, 186 in 15, the rows on
the host as on the iPad, "(unknown sender)", "" and 1970-01-01 with no
ids, and the kept rows refused as another letter's; in the whole suite
those 15 alone, the three that passed being the two listings with the
news ahead, whose last line was the letter's, and the letter not asked
for: nothing else held it. The parser not merging, `IMAPClient.ordered`
still merging, 39 in 5: every FETCH of one letter with the news ahead,
the kept rows and the labels, and the parser's own; the listings held,
merged there, and so did every FETCH of one letter with the news after
its line, the first line being the letter's. `ordered` not merging across
answers, 4 in 1, the two FETCHes. A summary with no ENVELOPE made a row,
15 in 2, the blank row on the list and on the kept page. The later FLAGS
taken only when not empty, 3 in 3; the later X-GM-LABELS taken whether
sent or not, 4 in 2; the parser not saying FLAGS came, 14 in 9. The
first line kept, 80 in 15. The smaller fix, lines with no ENVELOPE
dropped from a listing and nothing merged, 53 in 15: rows whole and their
marks stale, every FETCH of one letter as before, and nothing in the log
of what was left out. A line with nothing but flags laid over the line
before it, whatever its UID, 8 in 5.

And each item the earlier line keeps when the later one did not carry
it, undone one at a time. The arrival and the size taken from the later
line alone, 10 in 4: with the news ahead, the row has no arrival, the
letter is not kept as large and is opened whole, and its summary has no
size or arrival, in the parser's test too. The structure taken from the
later line alone, 23 in 4: with the news after the letter's line, the
row has no paperclip and no file, on the list and on the kept page, and
no preview; the letter in parts has no structure and nothing of its
text, a file is not found, and the summary has no structure, in the
parser's test too. The bytes taken from the later line alone, 10 in 2:
with the news after the line, the letter's bytes, named, asked and
plain, are empty, the letter in parts has no header and no text, a file
is not found and a preview is empty, in the parser's test too.

The full suite, serially: 1,874 tests, 5 skipped, none failing. The
release build for the iPad links.

**Not covered.**

- Seen on the iPad fixed, below, but for `\Flagged`, whose news is the
  same line: still to run on the test iPad (TODO).
- A listing from the top with a letter left out for no ENVELOPE comes back
  one short, which the list takes for the end of the folder until the next
  Refresh, as for a letter gone between the SEARCH and the FETCH. It needs
  a news line for a letter whose own line never came; not seen.
- A letter whose own line always came without its ENVELOPE would be left
  out of every listing, where it was a row with no sender. Gmail sends one
  whenever it is asked, and the parser reads any list there as one; the
  log line names the letter if it ever happens.
- News with no UID, which RFC 3501 allows outside a UID command, is left
  aside; Gmail's carries the UID.

**Seen on the test iPad, 2026-10-22**, a build of int9 (8607083), three
panes, Organize by Thread on, the test account; the letters made on the
host and put in its Inbox, their marks set from the host over IMAP and
Refresh tapped at once after each. Steps 1 to 3 of the TODO check passed
but for `\Flagged`, and B-102's step 3 with them. Of 34 Refreshes so
made, 13 had the news inside the listing's FETCH, after the letter's own
line and before the OK: on the conversation, on a single row and on
B-102's pair; three times the old flags in the letter's line and the new
in the news after it, and twice `FLAGS ()`. Every Refresh drew whole
rows, the conversation never split, with the new mark where the news
came inside the listing, the arrow, the forward arrow and the dot on and
off and the Inbox's count with them; `SESSION-IDENT` named a Gmail id
each time, and no `FETCH-NO-ENVELOPE` line came. The same STORE that
split the row in B-102's check, its news inside the listing this time,
kept it whole. `\Flagged` was not set from the host there; `$Forwarded`
stood in, its news the same line. `\Flagged`'s news inside the listing,
the flag on the row at that Refresh, is still to run on the test iPad.

## B-113 — FIXED 2026-10-22, found on the iPad and seen there fixed. The words after a file put among them, as Apple Mail sends one, were nowhere

**What he saw.** Seen on the test iPad on 2026-10-22, at B-101's check, step
7, with letters the host made and APPENDed to the test account's Inbox, and
again from a fresh start of the app with a letter made a second way. A
letter of Apple Mail's shape for a PDF put in the middle of the words:
multipart/alternative of the plain words and a multipart/mixed of an HTML
part, the PDF sent inline with no `Content-ID`, and an HTML part after it.
The pane showed the PDF's row in the header and the words before it,
"Words before the PDF: the programme is below.", and nothing more: "Words
after the PDF: see you on Thursday at two." and "Sent from my iPad" were
nowhere, in three panes and two, nor after a scroll. Only the list's
preview, made from the plain words, had them. The whole letter had come,
3,010 bytes in one FETCH, so they were lost in the decoding. The plain
multipart/mixed of the same, an HTML part, a PDF of 1 MB, and an HTML part
after it, lost its "Sent from my iPad" the same way. Mail shows every part
in order: the words, the file, the words after it.

**What it was.** `MIMEDecoder.chooseBodies` gave a letter one HTML part and
one plain part. In an alternative it took the last of each, the mixed for
the HTML; in a mixed, as in any multipart but an alternative, the first. So
the HTML was the words before the PDF, and the pane draws the HTML whenever
there is any, though the plain words had every one. `collectAttachments`
then dropped the HTML part after the PDF as an unnamed text part, "the
alternative we did not pick". Older than B-101, which left both as they
were; its host test held this result
(`testTheBodyOfALetterWithAFileSentInlineIsAsItWas`), and its Not covered
said so.

**Changed.**

1. *Every part of the words, in order* (`MIMEDecoder.bodyPlan(of:)`, in
   place of `chooseBodies`). A letter's body is the list of parts its HTML
   is made of and the list its plain words are, each in order. A mixed,
   and any multipart RFC 2046 has read as one, gives every part in its
   turn: words, a file, the words after it. An alternative gives, as
   before, the last of its alternatives with HTML for the HTML and the
   last with plain words for the plain words. A related, a signed, an
   encrypted and a report give the first part with words, as before: the
   rest are the pictures it shows, its signature, its key, the status and
   the letter a report is about. A text part with a name, which the header
   lists as a file (B-101), and one neither plain nor HTML, a calendar's
   ICS, are the letter's words only when it has no others, the first of
   them; beside other words the named ones are files and the others
   nothing, as they were.
2. *Joined* (`MIMEDecoder.joined`). A body of one part is that part's words
   exactly as they came, so a letter of one, nearly every letter, is byte
   for byte what it was. Of more, the HTML is each HTML part without its
   wrapper (`DocumentWrapper`, which the pane takes off anyway), with
   plain words in it as escaped text that keeps its lines; the plain words
   are each part on a line of its own, an HTML part as its text
   (`HTMLText`), as a reply quotes one. A body with no HTML part has no
   HTML, and one with no plain part no plain words, as before: the plain
   mixed above has no plain words, and a reply quotes its HTML's text,
   every word.
3. *The file where it sat.* In the HTML a file with words before it and
   after it leaves a mark in its place, a comment (`BodyFiles.mark`). The
   pane makes the mark of a file the header lists into the file's row,
   once, on a letter's own page and in a conversation's stack
   (`PanePage`, `BodyFiles.rows`): its name and size as the header's row
   writes them, in the letter's link colour, 44 pt tall, a link of the
   pane's own, `bmfile:`, that opens it in Quick Look as the header's row
   does (`PaneNavigation`'s `openFile`, `MessageDetailViewController`),
   the letter's own file or, in the stack, that letter's. No "Open this
   link?", nothing in Safari. The header keeps its row, grey from the tap
   and blue once the letter has come, as B-101 has it. A mark of anything
   else stays a comment: a picture the body shows by `cid:`
   (`isShownInBody`), a part the letter does not have, a second mark of
   the same file. A reply's quote takes it out with every other comment
   (`QuotedMarkup`), so it never goes on. A file before or after all of
   the words has no mark, and its row in the header alone, as every file
   always had; a plain letter has no row among its words.
4. *The header, the paperclip and the preview.* Every part shown as words
   is left out of the header's rows and the paperclip
   (`collectAttachments`, `IMAPMailRepository.hasAttachment`), where it was
   the two parts shown. So a text file sent inline after the words is a
   file, with its row and its paperclip, and no longer the plain words, as
   B-101's Not covered had it, a reply quoting the file in place of the
   letter. The preview is made from the first part of the plain words,
   where the letter begins: as before for every shape but HTML followed by
   a plain part, a list's footer say, which was previewed from the plain
   part and is now from the HTML.
5. *A letter too large to fetch whole* (above 5 MB, B-054). Each body's
   parts share the 2 MiB in turn (`MIMEDecoder.Allowance`): the first
   given all of it, as one part always was, each after it what those
   before it left. A part is fetched once, with the more of its two
   shares, and each body reads its own (`IMAPClient.fetchLetterInPart`
   takes the bytes of each section now). The sections go sixteen to a
   FETCH (`IMAPClient.sectionsPerFetch`), so a letter of its plain words
   and its HTML, nearly every one, is one FETCH after the first, where it
   was two, one for each; the FETCH's answer is read by section
   (`IMAPFetchResult.sections`). A fetch he has moved on from, which
   `PaneLoads` cancels, stops before its next FETCH with the connection
   up. The body is shown to where its fetch stopped and no further,
   nothing drawn after words cut short, not a file's mark nor a
   forwarded letter's lines, and the pane says it is only the beginning,
   as before.
6. *No more than a body holds,* found on the host since. A stranger can
   send a quarter of a million tiny parts of words, and every part drawn
   in its turn had a cost for each: a large letter made a FETCH for each,
   one after another on the one line, which moving to another letter did
   not stop; and every letter's walk made a list of copies of its parts
   for each multipart, copied again into the one above, for both bodies,
   and again for each row's preview and paperclip. A letter of 250,000 parts,
   3.2 MB, took 2.6 s and 300 MB more than the letter itself to decode in
   a release build, against 0.19 s and nothing before. Now a body holds
   at most 64 parts of words (`MIMEDecoder.maxBodyWords`), and 256
   pieces of every kind (`maxBodyPieces`), the files among the words and
   the forwarded letters' lines with them; a body with more is drawn to
   the last it holds, nothing after it, and the pane says it is only the
   beginning (`DecodedBody.isShortened`, for a letter fetched whole too,
   and so a reply's quote says so as well). Both bodies are walked in one
   pass, each into one list (`MIMEDecoder.Walk`), and a choice that needs
   to know what a part holds, an alternative's, a related's, a mixed's
   with a named text part in it, asks it (`Holds`), which makes nothing.
   The forwarded letter's ENVELOPE is held by reference
   (`MIMEPart.Envelope`), as inline it made every part of every tree 280
   bytes where it was 168. Mail on an iPad splits a letter's HTML into
   one part more than the files put among its words, so 64 parts is a
   letter with 63 files among them.

**Not changed.** What a file is: `MIMEPart.isAttachment`, `isListedFile`
and `Attachment.isShownInBody`. The header's rows and the paperclip for
every shape B-101's table holds. The quote bars, which are rules over
whatever the HTML holds. The copy kept on the iPad, rows alone: its format,
and a row kept from before, until its folder is next listed from the top.
Search, which Gmail makes of every part. Send.

**What he sees.** A letter from Mail on an iPad or an iPhone with a PDF put
among its words: the words before it, the PDF's name and size in blue on a
line of its own where it sat, the words after it, and "Sent from my iPad"
at the end. A tap on the blue name opens the PDF, as the row in the header
does. Reply and Forward quote every word. A letter whose HTML has a plain
footer after it, as a mailing list adds, shows the footer. A text file sent

## B-114 — FIXED 2026-10-22, found on the iPad and seen there fixed. A letter forwarded inline after a note was nowhere: not its words, its From or its Subject, and no row

**What he saw.** Seen on the test iPad on 2026-10-22, at B-101's check, a
shape beyond step 9's own, with letters the host made and APPENDed to the
test account's Inbox, and again from a fresh start of the app with a letter
made a second way. A note, and then the letter it forwards, sent inline as
message/rfc822 with no name: multipart/mixed of a text/plain note and a
message/rfc822 part, `Content-Disposition: inline`, holding a plain letter.
It is what mutt's `mime_forward` sends. The pane showed the note, "My own
note above the forwarded letter.", and nothing more: the forwarded letter's
words, its From and its Subject were nowhere, with no row in the header and
no paperclip on its list row, in three panes and two. The whole letter had
come. He could not reach the forwarded letter at all. Mail draws it after
the note.

**What it was.** `chooseBodies` walked into the forwarded letter and found
its words, but in the mixed it kept the first plain part, the note, and
dropped them. `collectAttachments` walked into it too, and dropped its
unnamed text part. And a message/rfc822 part sent inline is words in the
body, never a file (`isListedFile`, B-101): no row and no paperclip. A
forwarded letter with nothing before it was shown, its words being the
first. Older than B-101. Found on the host with it: a note before a
forwarded letter of HTML showed the forwarded HTML alone, without the note,
the note being the first plain part and the letter's HTML the first HTML.
Six of the thirty ordinary letters the suite makes are such forwards.

**Changed.**

1. *After the note.* B-113's body of every part in order: a letter
   forwarded inline is its own body, by the rules any letter's goes by,
   after what comes before it. Its pictures show by `cid:`, and its own
   files are listed with their paperclip, as before; it is no file itself.
2. *Its header lines above its words, in Mail's form*
   (`MIMEDecoder.ForwardedFields`): "Begin forwarded message:", a blank
   line, then From, Date, To, Cc when it has one, and Subject, and a blank
   line after them; in the HTML each label bold and the subject's value
   bold, as `AppleMailHTML` writes a Forward. They are the lines this
   app's own Forward writes of the same letter (`Draft.forwarding`,
   B-050), its Date in the iPad's zone. A field the letter has nothing in
   is left out.
3. *From where.* From the forwarded letter's own header, in the part's
   bytes, for a letter downloaded; from the ENVELOPE its BODYSTRUCTURE
   carries for one too large to fetch whole, which the parser now keeps on
   the part (`MIMEPart.envelope`). Nothing more is fetched for them, and
   they are the same lines.
4. *Only with words outside it.* A letter that is nothing but the one it
   forwards reads as it did, its words alone (B-101's step 9, seen so on
   the iPad).
5. *A note of plain words before a letter of HTML:* the pane draws the
   HTML, the note in it as escaped text that keeps its lines, then the
   header lines, then the forwarded letter's markup; the plain words are
   the note, the lines and the letter's plain words.
6. *Sent under an encoding,* found on the host since. A forwarded letter
   sent base64 or quoted-printable, which RFC 2046 does not allow but
   mail programs send, was read as it came, and its encoded lines were
   drawn as its words under the note. It is read with its encoding undone
   now (`MIMEDecoder.parseNode`), and its header lines from its header
   undone too; once on the way down, so the copy made is the letter's
   size at most. Its bytes are kept as they came, for a tap on its row
   when it is a file, which undoes the encoding as for any file.
7. *A broken multipart inside,* found on the host since. A forwarded
   letter whose multipart has no boundary that appears, or is past the
   nesting cap, is read as one part of words, as before; but it was
   numbered with the letter's own number, and its words took the place of
   the letter's bytes: its header lines were read from its words, found
   none, and the forwarded words ran on from the note as if they were
   part of it. It is numbered as one part is, 2.1 under the letter's 2,
   and the letter's bytes are the letter's, for its lines and for a tap on
   its row when it is a file (which before opened its words alone).
8. *Named and sent inline,* decided since. A message/rfc822 with a name
   and `Content-Disposition: inline` is drawn under the note as any
   forwarded letter sent inline is, with no row and no paperclip, by the
   rule every file goes by (`MIMEPart.isAttachment`: inline is the
   sender's word that it be shown). It was not a row before either: alone
   its words were the body, and after a note it was lost. With a name and
   no disposition, or sent as an attachment, it is a file, as before.

**Not changed.** A letter forwarded as a file, named with no disposition,
or sent as an attachment, named or not: a row, `forwarded.eml` or
`attachment-2.eml`, and the paperclip, as before, nothing of it in the
body, its row opening it as any file's does. A forwarded letter with
nothing before it. A report's returned letter, not drawn, as before. The
Forward he writes.

**What he sees.** A note with a letter forwarded after it: the note, then
"Begin forwarded message:", the forwarded letter's From, Date, To and
Subject, then its words, and its files in the header with the paperclip.
Reply and Forward quote all of it. No new words: "Begin forwarded message:"
is what his own forwards say.

**Tests.** `BodyInOrderTests`, seven for this: the note, the header lines
and the forwarded words, nothing listed, no paperclip, the preview the
note's, and a reply quoting all three in order; the same sent as base64,
as the second run on the iPad was; a forwarded letter of HTML, the note as
text in the HTML, the lines, the letter's markup, and the plain words the

writes of the same letter, plain and HTML; the forwarded letter's own PDF
listed with its paperclip, and words of its own in a text part with a
name, in the body with no row or paperclip; a letter forwarded as a file,
named and sent as an attachment, unnamed and sent as one, and named with
no disposition, each a row with the paperclip and the body the note; and a
letter that is only the one it forwards, its words and no lines.
`LargeLetterTests`, one, over the shipping repository and the scripted
server: a note, a forwarded letter and a PDF over the limit, the note and

same in every zone: in New York's they pass, and without that they fail.

Each rule undone by hand, the same classes as B-113's run, then put back
and passing: header lines never drawn, 9 in 6; drawn for a letter that is

**Seen on the test iPad, 2026-10-22**, three panes and two, against the
test account on Gmail, with letters the host made and APPENDed to its
Inbox (TODO, B-114's check): steps 1 to 5 and 7 to 9 passed; in 4, Quick
Look could not show `forwarded.eml`, saying only that it is data, 454

stayed grey and the header read "To: me". A second tap, and two panes, the

of 8.9 MB with a PDF and no forward, which takes the same way. The app's
log had the letter's structure come, and then `UID FETCH <uid> (UID
BODY.PEEK[1]<0.2097152> BODY.PEEK[2.1]<0.2097070>)` answered "NO Some
messages could not be FETCHed (Failure)". Asked from the host, read only,
Gmail gave BODY[1], BODY[2], BODY[2.HEADER], BODY[2.MIME], BODY[3] and
BODY[2.TEXT], the forwarded words, and refused BODY[2.1], with a range or
without; [1] with [2.1] in one FETCH, refused, and [1] with [2.TEXT],
both. The same refusal cost a list its previews: Trash's FETCH of
BODY.PEEK[1.1] for eleven letters, one of them step 5's lone forward, had
the other ten's data and then NO, and a row beside it that had shown "A
PDF attached after the words..." showed no preview.

*What it was.* RFC 3501 numbers the body of a message/rfc822 part that is
one part, not a multipart, 2.1 under the letter's 2, and gives the same
bytes as 2.TEXT. Gmail serves only the second. The parser numbered it 2.1
(as `MIMEDecoder` numbers it for a letter fetched whole, which reply,
forward, a file's row and a kept copy go by), and every FETCH asked for it
by that number. A letter at or under 5 MB is opened by fetching it whole,
so only a large one could not be opened; a list's previews ask for any
letter's part. And `fetchLetterInPart` took any answer but OK to its FETCH
of the parts as a connection lost, so one part refused cost the whole
letter, the note with it, blamed on the connection. A preview FETCH
answered NO was thrown away whole, though its doc said it kept what came.
The scripted server answered BODY[2.1], so no test met Gmail's refusal.

*Changed.*

1. *Asked for by the name Gmail serves.* The parser marks that body
   (`MIMEPart.isMessageText`), and every FETCH asks for it as 2.TEXT
   (`MIMEPart.fetchSection`): the parts of a large letter, a list row's
   preview (a lone forward's words are 1.TEXT, asked for apart from the
   1.1 of a plain and HTML pair), and a file that is the whole of a
   forwarded letter, both while the letter is the one last opened and when
   its structure is fetched again. Its number stays 2.1 everywhere else.
   A forwarded letter whose body is a multipart is asked for by its
   parts' numbers, as before.
2. *A part refused costs that part.* A FETCH of a large letter's parts
   answered NO keeps what came, asks for each part that did not come
   alone, and leaves out one refused alone too (`LetterInPart.refused`):
   the rest of the letter is drawn around it (with the note refused, the
   forwarded letter's lines and words; with the forwarded words refused,
   the note and the lines), and the pane says "Only the beginning of this
   message is shown.", the notice a letter cut short has. HTML the parts
   refused leave with nothing to show gives way to plain words that came:
   the plain words are drawn under the notice. A letter none of whose
   words came, its one part refused or every part, fails as a refused
   FETCH failed it before: "This message could not be downloaded. Check
   the connection and tap it again." Gmail's NO can be a passing failure,
   and an empty letter would give him nothing to tap again for. A
   connection that drops fails the letter as before, after the one try
   more on a new connection every read has, in the FETCH of the parts or
   in one of a part asked for alone.
3. *A preview refused costs that row.* A preview FETCH answered NO keeps
   every letter's data that came with it (`fetchPartialBodies`). The FETCH
   of his Sent Mail's lines in a conversation (B-104,
   `fetchPartialBodiesWhileOpen`) was written apart from this change, and
   throws them away still: where the two are merged it must keep them too
   (TODO, B-114), and a test here fails until it does. Kept where merged,
   2026-10-23.
4. *Never "no text" for a letter shown in part.* A letter shown only in
   part is never said to have no text (`PanePage.isEmpty`): its page, and
   its body in a conversation, are the notice over whatever came.

*Tests.* The scripted server serves a letter as Gmail does
(`ScriptedIMAPServer.deliver(described:)`): the one-part body of a
forwarded letter as 2.TEXT, and a FETCH asking 2.1 of it answered NO,
nothing sent of that letter and every other letter's as asked; and it can
drop the connection at a FETCH of a part (`hangsUpOnSections`).
`LargeLetterTests`' forward over the limit now expects BODY.PEEK[2.TEXT],
every FETCH answered OK and the letter whole; four more there: a part
refused, the note and the lines shown, each part asked for alone, said to
be only the beginning, one connection; the note refused, the lines and the
forwarded words shown; the connection dropped at the parts, "Can't
connect" after a second connection, nothing asked alone; and a scan that
is the whole of a forwarded letter, its row 2.1 and its bytes
BODY.PEEK[2.TEXT], in this launch and the next. `RepositoryWireTests`,
two: a lone forward's preview asked for as 1.TEXT apart from a 1.1 beside
it, both rows with their previews; and one row's preview refused in a
shared FETCH, the other keeping its own. `IMAPParserTests`, one: the body
numbered 2.1 and asked for as 2.TEXT, a forwarded multipart's parts, the
letter, the note and a file by their numbers, and a letter that is itself
a message/rfc822, 1.1 as 1.TEXT.

With the tip's own client, parser and repository and these tests, all

then put back and passing, counted as failures in tests: the body never

of the parts failing the letter, 2 in 2; a refused part not left out, 4 in
2 (with the note refused the body was empty and not said to be short); a
dropped connection taken for a refusal, 3 in 1; previews asked for by

the letter last opened asked for by number, 1 in 1; and one fetched with
its structure, 1 in 1.

The full suite, serially: 1,904 tests, 5 skipped, none failing. The
release build for the iPad links. Step 6, and step 5's list with its

2026-10-23, below).

*Changed again, 2026-10-22, the same day, before the iPad saw it.* As
first changed, a large letter whose only words were refused, its one part
or the note and the letter it forwards, came to the pane as an empty
letter said to be short: "This message has no text." for the one part,
since the pane drew an empty letter as one whatever it was said to be,
and the forwarded letter's header lines alone under the notice for the
two. Before, the same NO had said it could not be downloaded, and a tap
again could bring it. The HTML of a plain and HTML pair refused alone
drew the empty HTML, the notice over nothing, the plain words that came
not shown. And a connection that dropped while a refused part was asked
for alone could be taken for a refusal with nothing to show it: the
scripted server dropped it only at the FETCH of all the parts. Now the
letter with no words fails as it did, the HTML gives way to the plain
words, a letter shown in part is never "no text" (2 and 4 above), and
the letter's plan gives each part by the name it is asked for by, its
bytes kept and read back under that name, so the structure is not
searched again for each part.

*Tests, again.* The scripted server can drop the connection only at a
FETCH of one section alone (`hangsUpOnSectionsAlone`). `LargeLetterTests`,
four more: the forwarded words refused and the connection dropped when
they are asked for alone, "Can't connect" after a second connection, the
same FETCHes there; a letter of one part of words refused, "Can't
connect", that part asked once and on the one connection; the note and
the forwarded words both refused, the same; and the HTML of a pair
refused, the plain words under the notice, no HTML. `PanePageTests`, one:
a letter with nothing in it, said to be short, has a page and a stack body
with the notice and never "This message has no text.", and the same
letter whole still has it. `RepositoryWireTests`, one: read from the
client's source, no FETCH of previews looks at its status, so the one of
B-104 fails it on a merge until it keeps what came.

Each change undone by hand, those run, then put back and passing: the
letter with no words not failed, 2 failures in 2 tests; the pane drawing
a short letter as having no text, 1 in 1; the HTML kept, 2 in 1; the HTML
given way but not said to be short, 2 in 1; a drop at a part asked for
alone swallowed as a refusal, 4 in 1; the plan naming each part by its
number, 15 in 5; its bytes read back by its number, 3 in 2; a part
refused looked for by its number, 2 in 1; and a preview FETCH that looks
at its status, 2 in 2.

The full suite, serially: 1,910 tests, 5 skipped, none failing. The
release build for the iPad links. Step 6 and step 5's list are still to
be run again on the iPad, and a forward of a forward with them (TODO):
run again 2026-10-23, below.

**Not covered.**

- How Mail's reading pane draws a forwarded letter, a box or a line about
  it, the lines as here or others: not compared on a screen. The lines are
  the ones Mail's Forward writes (high confidence for those), and "Begin
  forwarded message:" is Mail's word for a forward, not a word read from
  its pane drawing one.
- A letter that is only the one it forwards has no header lines, as
  before; Mail may draw them.
- A digest (multipart/digest), whose parts are letters with no
  `Content-Type` of their own: the parser reads such a part as plain
  text, so each is drawn as words, its header among them, all of them now
  where the first was before. Not seen in his mail.
- A subject folded across lines: the envelope's and the header's can
  differ by a space, so a large letter's lines may not be the whole
  letter's to the byte.
- A forwarded letter sent under an encoding inside one whose encoding was
  undone: read as it came, its encoded lines drawn as its words, so that
  no letter costs more than one copy of itself to read.
- A letter too large to fetch whole that forwards one under an encoding:
  drawn from the server's structure of it, as the server reads it. Not
  tried against Gmail.
- A forwarded letter whose body is a multipart, in a letter too large to
  fetch whole: its parts asked for as 2.1 and 2.2, which RFC 3501 gives
  them; Gmail served them under a message/rfc822 on the iPad, 2026-10-23.
  A refusal there costs those parts alone now, said to be only the
  beginning.
- A forward of a forward over 5 MB, a message/rfc822 whose body is itself
  one: the words of the letter inside it asked for as 2.1.TEXT, RFC 3501's
  name. Gmail refuses `BODY[2.1.TEXT]`, alone and beside `[1]`, and
  serves those words as `BODY[2.1]` (seen 2026-10-23, below). So it shows
  the notice and loses the innermost words: the note and both header
  blocks are shown, the second with nothing under it. Asking that name
  for such a body would show them; not changed.
- Which parts Gmail refuses beyond these is not known; any is left out of
  the letter, the rest shown, and not asked for again under another name.
  A letter none of whose words come fails as one that could not be
  downloaded, every time if the refusal is for good.
- The HTML of a plain and HTML pair refused, the plain words shown in its
  place: a picture only the HTML shows by `cid:` is in neither, and is
  not listed as a file either. Not seen.
- A letter forwarded with a name and sent inline is drawn, not a row,
  decided here by the rule every file goes by; how Mail draws one is not
  compared on a screen. A row, if the owner wants one for a named
  letter whatever its disposition, is `isAttachment` asking for a name
  of a message/rfc822 part, and its test.

- *5's list.* Six letters on one page, the lone forward among them: every

## B-115 — FIXED 2026-10-23, found on the iPad and seen there fixed. Go to Date landed at the foot of a folder whose first letters are dated later, whatever day was asked

**What he saw.** Seen on the test iPad on 2026-10-23, in the size test's
round (TODO, gap review), a build of int12 (140df65), three panes and two,
and made again from a fresh start of the app the same morning. The test
account had been filled with made-up letters APPENDed already read, each
arriving, as Gmail says, when its Date says, after the account's own
letters: an Inbox of 57,209 and a Sent Mail of 24,026. Every Go to Date
jump, Current Mailbox, landed at the very foot of the folder, on the
account's own first letter, UID 1, dated 25 August 2026, and the status
line said "Showing August 25": 10 March 2014, a day of five letters;
1 June 2012; 1 January 2011, before the oldest letter, 4 January 2012; and
14 August 2026, the newest day of the letters copied in, at the top of
the Inbox. In Sent Mail, 15 May 2019 landed on the account's own first
sent letter, "Showing September 19". The app's log had each SEARCH
answered `* ESEARCH (TAG …) UID MIN 1`, and the same SEARCHes asked read
only from the host gave the same. A jump to 20 October said "No mail on or
after October 20", as it should.

Not by design: a jump opens at the first letter of the day asked for. In
his own mailbox, sampled read only back to 2009, every letter arrived on
the day it is dated, so his Inbox, as sampled, would not have shown it; a
folder whose letters came in another order shows it on every jump.

**What it was.** A jump asked one SEARCH, every letter dated on or after
the day (`IMAPDate.sentOnOrAfter`, with B-058's bounds on when it
arrived): `UID SEARCH RETURN (MIN) SENTSINCE "10-Mar-2014" SINCE
"03-Mar-2014" BEFORE "31-Oct-2026"`. `PageWindow.anchor` took the lowest
UID it matched, the letter that came into the folder first, and the docs
said that is "the oldest … the first to have arrived". It is the first of
the day only while the folder's letters came in the order they were
written. On the test account the account's own letters came first, UIDs 1
to 394, dated August to October 2026: they matched every day before then,
and the first of them won every jump. `PageWindow.landing` kept it, being
on or after the day and not more than a week ahead, and with newer letters
above it in the window "No mail on or after" was never said either. Older
than B-058, which bounded the same SEARCH by arrival and left which UID
it took alone; B-063 asked for the lowest alone.

The same shape is ordinary outside the test: a Gmail label's UIDs go by
when the label was put on, mail imported or copied into Gmail comes in the
order it was copied, and a letter moved back into the Inbox takes a new
UID.

**Changed.**

1. *His day first, by its letters' dates* (`IMAPDate.jump`,
   `IMAPClient.PageSearch.lowestDated`). A jump asks first for every
   letter of the days, as Gmail counts them from midnight UTC (B-058),
   that hold any of his day (`IMAPDate.sentOnHisDay`); in New York the
   day and the next: `UID SEARCH SENTSINCE "10-Mar-2014" SENTBEFORE
   "12-Mar-2014" SINCE "03-Mar-2014" BEFORE "31-Oct-2026"`, with B-058's
   bounds on when it arrived as before. It is asked whole, a plain
   SEARCH: two days' letters, a few dozen in his Inbox. Their dates are
   fetched in the same hold, `UID FETCH … (UID INTERNALDATE ENVELOPE)`,
   each the date its row shows, the Date or with none when it arrived; a
   letter given with no ENVELOPE, which is never made a row, is left out.
   The anchor is the lowest UID of those dated within his day, midnight
   to midnight where he is: a letter of his day however the folder is
   ordered, and the day's first while its letters came in order.
2. *After it only while it has none.* With none, his evening before
   alone or no letter at all, the letters after his day within two days
   of it, then four, eight, and so on, doubling
   (`IMAPDate.sentAfterHisDay`), each asked for its lowest UID alone as
   before (B-063), the first to match anything giving the anchor and
   none after it asked. They begin at the day of Gmail's that his next
   midnight falls in, `SENTSINCE "16-Mar-2014"` for Saturday the 15th in
   New York, which begins after his own midnight: nothing of his evening
   before is in them, and his day had none.
3. *Bounded.* At most fifteen SEARCHes before the one with no end
   (`IMAPDate.spanSearches`): his day and spans to 16,384 days, some 44
   years, and none reaching the day before which every letter matched
   has arrived, a week after today (the `BEFORE`). Then, last, every
   letter after his day, with no end. So a day with mail is one dated
   SEARCH and one FETCH of dates; the day after the newest letter is his
   day, the spans that fit before a week from today and that SEARCH, and
   says "No mail on or after" as before; and no jump asks more than
   sixteen, for a day more than 44 years before the oldest letter. A day
   a week or more ahead, which the picker does not offer, asks the one
   SEARCH a jump asked before, alone.
4. *In one hold.* All of them, and the FETCH of the dates, in the one
   hold of the connection that has the listing's `UID SEARCH ALL` and the
   window's FETCH, after the one SELECT, so the anchor and the listing
   stay in one numbering. Each span is asked as one alone was (B-063):
   `RETURN (MIN)` where the server advertises ESEARCH, plainly where it
   does not or refuses RETURN. A SEARCH refused whole fails the jump, as
   before, with nothing after it asked, and so does a FETCH of the dates
   that gives none of them.
5. The docs that said the lowest UID is the day's first letter
   (`IMAPDate`, `PageWindow.anchor`, `MailRepository.messages(around:)`,
   `IMAPClient.performLowest`) say what it is, and `PageWindow.landing`'s
   what is left for it to move.

*Why the dates.* The fix as first written asked for Gmail's day alone,
`SENTSINCE "10-Mar-2014" SENTBEFORE "11-Mar-2014"`, and took its lowest
UID. Gmail's day runs from midnight UTC, so in New York it holds his
evening before, from 8 pm in summer and 7 pm in winter, and in a folder
whose UIDs do not follow its dates a letter of that evening can be the
lowest: taken, `PageWindow.landing` moved up from it to the next letter
above it dated on or after his day, which in such a folder can be of any
year. Found after it was written, with a scratch test in New York: a
letter of 9.30 pm on 9 March 2014, then one of 1 January 2020, then one
of 11 am on the 10th, and a jump to the 10th said "Showing January 1,
2020"; a Friday evening's letter did the same to the Saturday after it.
East of Greenwich Gmail's day holds his next morning's first hours and
misses his own, and the jump landed on the next morning. Folders in date
order, as his Inbox was sampled, landed right either way.

**Not changed.** `PageWindow`: the window around the anchor, ten rows
above it at most and the rest older (*since B-117 fetched with the page
above it, `PageWindow.jumpWindow`*), and the landing by his calendar
(B-058), which now seldom has anything to move. "Showing" the day of the
letter landed on; "No mail on or after" that day; the day and the scope
remembered; Sent Mail and every other folder alike, and All Mailboxes
jumping in All Mail; a jump called off by another tap; the kept copy,
which keeps no jump (D-016); Go to Date offline, its alert as before,
nothing sent. The listing's `UID SEARCH ALL`. No new words.

**What he sees.** A jump opens on a letter of the day he picked,
"Showing" that day, in any folder, whatever order its letters came into
it: the day's first where they came in the order written, as in his
Inbox as sampled, and otherwise the one of the day that came into the
folder first. On a day with no mail, at a letter of the first days after
it that have any, the first of them where the letters came in order, as
before. Before the oldest letter of the test account, at the oldest,
where it landed at the foot. *With Organize by Thread on, a letter that
begins a conversation is in its conversation's row, dated as the
conversation's newest letter, up the list where that letter puts it, and
since B-118 the list opens on the oldest row dated on or after the day, as
Mail's list shows it: 1 June 2012's first letter in the test account's
Inbox is answered on 5 June, and the day's next letter, 763, is on top.
B-117 opened on the conversation's row.*

**Tests.** `GoToDateOrderTests`, seventeen, over the shipping repository
and client against the scripted server. Twelve on an Inbox like the test

The weekend: the Monday's first, after three SEARCHes, the spans from the
Sunday. A day before the oldest letter: the oldest, at the tenth SEARCH,
a span of 512 days, as on the test account. One in 1990, 21 years before

15 May 2019 and 10 March 2014. All Mail, landing, searching and holding

mail after a letter of 9.30 pm the evening before and one of 2020, and a

that showed it, each landing on his day's letter, or the Monday's, where

in Tokyo, a day with mail after his next morning's letter of 1 am and one
of 2020, and a day whose one letter is of 3 am, Gmail's day before, below
one of 2020 and the next day's. Each of the seventeen reads off the
connection log every command from the SELECT on: his day's SEARCH, the
FETCH of its letters' dates where it matched any, the spans, the listing
and the window's FETCH, in one hold, nothing between them, on one

winter and summer, in New York, in Tokyo and across a year; the spans

the lowest UID dated within it, not the lowest of all, the day asked

With the first version's three parts put back by hand, Gmail's day alone,
